title: What is data skew in Spark — when one partition has disproportionately more data than others (a "hot key"), causing one task to run much longer than the rest — and how do you detect it (Spark UI: one task takes 10-100x longer, shuffle read/write imbalanced)?
shortTitle: Data skew in Spark — hot keys and how to detect it

s1_definition.profdef: Data skew in Spark occurs when data is distributed unevenly across partitions after a shuffle, so one or a few partitions hold far more records than the rest — usually because a particular join or group key, the hot key, appears disproportionately often. Since Spark runs one task per partition, the oversized partition's task runs much longer than the others, becoming a straggler that delays the whole stage even though most tasks finished quickly. You detect it in the Spark UI by seeing one task take ten to a hundred times longer than the median, with correspondingly large and imbalanced shuffle read and write sizes.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine distributing the day's transactions to clerks by account number. Most accounts have a few transactions, but one corporate mega-account has millions. The clerk handling that mega-account is buried for hours while every other clerk finishes in minutes and sits idle. The whole batch is not done until that one overloaded clerk finishes. That one account is the hot key, and the imbalance is data skew.
s1_definition.oneliner: Data skew is one partition holding far more data than the rest due to a hot key, creating a straggler task — spot it in the Spark UI as one task taking ten to a hundred times longer with lopsided shuffle sizes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Data skew in Spark occurs when data is distributed unevenly across partitions after a shuffle, so one or a few partitions hold far more records than the rest — usually because a particular join or group key, the hot key, appears disproportionately often. Since Spark runs one task per partition, the oversized partition's task runs much longer than the others, becoming a straggler that delays the whole stage even though most tasks finished quickly. You detect it in the Spark UI by seeing one task take ten to a hundred times longer than the median, with correspondingly large and imbalanced shuffle read and write sizes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine distributing the day's transactions to clerks by account number. Most accounts have a few transactions, but one corporate mega-account has millions. The clerk handling that mega-account is buried for hours while every other clerk finishes in minutes and sits idle. The whole batch is not done until that one overloaded clerk finishes. That one account is the hot key, and the imbalance is data skew.

**One line to remember:** Data skew is one partition holding far more data than the rest due to a hot key, creating a straggler task — spot it in the Spark UI as one task taking ten to a hundred times longer with lopsided shuffle sizes.

sections.s2_technical:
Skew arises at shuffle boundaries. When Spark performs a wide operation like a join or a groupBy, it shuffles rows so that all rows for the same key land in the same partition. If the key distribution is uneven — a few keys account for most of the rows — then the partitions receiving those keys become huge while the others stay small. Because Spark schedules exactly one task per partition, the huge partition gets one task that must process all those rows, and that task takes far longer than its peers. The stage cannot complete until its slowest task finishes, so a single hot key can dominate the runtime, wasting the cluster as other executors sit idle.

The practical symptoms are distinctive. In the Spark UI's Stages tab, you open the stage and look at the task summary. With skew, the maximum task duration is wildly larger than the median — ten, fifty, or a hundred times. The same tab shows shuffle read and write per task, and the straggler task shows a shuffle read far larger than the others, confirming it received a disproportionate share of data. The event timeline shows most tasks finishing early and one running on alone. Sometimes the skewed task also spills to disk or fails with out-of-memory, because it cannot hold its oversized partition in memory.

Detecting the hot key itself usually means profiling the key distribution: grouping by the join or group key and counting rows per key reveals the dominant values. In banking this is often a known business reality — a sweep account, a suspense account, a default placeholder id, or a null key that collects all unmatched rows. Null or default keys are a classic skew source because every row lacking a real key piles into the same partition.

A senior-level nuance is distinguishing skew from simply having too few partitions. Too few partitions makes every task large but roughly equal; skew makes one task large while others are tiny. The fix differs: more partitions helps the former, but skew needs targeted handling like Adaptive Query Execution's skew join optimization, salting, or isolating the hot key. Another nuance is that skew can be hidden until data grows or a particular customer becomes dominant, so monitoring task-duration ratios over time catches emerging skew before it causes incidents. You also watch for skew in writes, where a partitionBy on a skewed column produces one gigantic output file.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India groups the day's transactions by account id to compute per-account totals. One corporate sweep account, SAV2001 acting as a pooling account, has the overwhelming majority of transactions. After the shuffle, its partition is enormous and its task runs a hundred times longer than the rest. This is classic data skew from a hot key.

Problem 2 — The engineer must detect it before fixing it. They look at the per-partition row counts and the task-duration ratio, identifying the straggler and the hot key. This mirrors reading the Spark UI task summary.

The demo computes row counts per partition after a simulated shuffle by account, finds the maximum-to-median ratio, flags skew, and identifies the hot key, logging the detection just as you would read the Spark UI.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five partitions after shuffling transactions by account id, with four partitions around ten thousand rows and one partition holding 2.4 million rows for the pooling account SAV2001.

Step 1: The detector computes the median partition size by sorting the counts and taking the middle value, which is about eleven thousand rows — representative of the normal partitions.

Step 2: It finds the heaviest partition, number two, dominated by SAV2001 with 2.4 million rows.

Step 3: It computes the max-to-median ratio, roughly 218 times, far above the skew threshold of ten.

Step 4: Because the ratio exceeds the threshold, it flags data skew and identifies SAV2001 as the hot key whose task will straggle about two hundred times longer, mirroring what the Spark UI task summary would show — one task far slower with a huge shuffle read.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:57:00 [INFO] Median partition size: 11000 rows
2026-10-30 04:57:00 [INFO] Heaviest partition: #2 key=SAV2001 rows=2400000
2026-10-30 04:57:00 [INFO] Max/median ratio: 218.2x
2026-10-30 04:57:00 [SEVERE] DATA SKEW DETECTED: task for partition 2 (hot key SAV2001) will straggle ~218x longer
2026-10-30 04:57:00 [WARNING] Spark UI would show this one task 10-100x slower with huge shuffle read.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Data skew in Spark is when data is distributed unevenly across partitions after a shuffle, so one or a few partitions hold far more records than the rest, almost always because a particular join or group key — the hot key — appears disproportionately often. Since Spark runs exactly one task per partition, the oversized partition's task runs much longer than its peers and becomes a straggler; the stage cannot finish until its slowest task finishes, so a single hot key can dominate the runtime while the rest of the cluster sits idle.

I detect it primarily in the Spark UI. On the Stages tab I open the stage and read the task summary, comparing the maximum task duration to the median. With skew the maximum is wildly larger — ten, fifty, even a hundred times the median — and the same tab shows that the straggler task has a far larger shuffle read than the others, confirming it received a disproportionate share of data. The event timeline shows most tasks finishing early and one running on alone, and the skewed task often spills to disk or even fails with out-of-memory because its partition does not fit in memory. To find the hot key itself I profile the distribution by grouping on the join or group key and counting rows per key, which surfaces the dominant values.

At the National Bank of India this was a recurring reality. When we grouped transactions by account id, a corporate pooling account held the overwhelming majority of transactions, so its partition was hundreds of times larger than the others and its task straggled while everything else was done. Null or default keys were another classic source, because every row without a real key piled into one partition. The distinction I always draw is that skew is one task large while the others are tiny, which is different from simply having too few partitions where every task is large but roughly equal — so skew needs targeted handling like Adaptive Query Execution's skew join optimization, salting, or isolating the hot key, rather than just adding more partitions. And because skew can emerge as data grows or a customer becomes dominant, I monitor the task-duration ratio over time to catch it before it causes an incident.
